mercy_translation.text:
Like a good teacher who cares for his students and, when they are unable to benefit from higher things, comes down to teach them through simpler things, so also does the Word of God. As Paul says, “Since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of the proclamation to save those who believe.”

For human beings had turned away from the contemplation of God and, as though sunk in a deep abyss with their eyes directed downward, were seeking God among created and sensible things, fashioning mortal human beings and demons as gods for themselves. For this reason the loving and common Savior of all, the Word of God, takes to himself a body, lives among human beings as a human being, and engages the senses of all. Thus those who imagined that God existed among bodily things might, from what the Lord accomplished through bodily works, understand the truth from those very works and through him come to think of the Father.

Being human and thinking in human ways, whatever they turned their senses toward, they found themselves met there and taught the truth from every side.

If they were captivated by creation, they saw creation confessing Christ as Lord. If their minds were preoccupied with human beings so that they regarded them as gods, then by comparing the Savior's works with theirs, the Savior alone among human beings was shown to be the Son of God, for none of those others had done such things as were done by the Word of God.

If they were preoccupied with demons, when they saw them driven out by the Lord, they learned that he alone is the Word of God and that the demons are not gods.

If their minds were already occupied with the dead so that they worshiped heroes and the gods spoken of by poets, when they saw the Savior's resurrection they confessed those others to be false and the Lord alone to be true—the Word of the Father, who is also Lord over death.

For this reason he was born and appeared as a human being, died and rose again, dimming and overshadowing the deeds of every human being who had ever lived by his own works, so that wherever human beings had been preoccupied he might raise them up from there and teach them his true Father. As he himself says, “I came to save and to seek what was lost.”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius' argument is pedagogical: Christ meets humanity at the level of the sensible in order to lead it to knowledge of the Father.
The chapter links miracles, exorcisms, resurrection, and the Incarnation as signs adapted to different forms of human error.
